extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and readers concerned with the moral purpose and social function of art
extracted.subtask_description: Articulate normative criteria for what counts as 'true' or good art: its purpose, audience, subject-matter, style, and social effects. The page argues standards against æsthetic theories that reduce art to beauty or pleasure and gives positive and negative tests for art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of art — transmission of highest and best feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a human activity whose purpose is the transmission to others of the highest and best feelings to which men have risen (particularly those flowing from religious perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy treats the transmission of feeling as the defining purpose: genuine art must transfer fresh, important feelings to others. Antipatterns: works made merely to display skill, to amuse, or to afford refined enjoyment without transmitting higher feelings. Examples: true art historically arose from prophets and religiously inspired writers; contrast with upper-class art that aims only at pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should serve goodness / have moral influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art is good when it serves goodness as understood by a society; art must contribute to moral improvement and the spread of good feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy notes ancient thinkers (e.g., Aristotle's catharsis) demanded moral influence from art. Art's value is tied to whether it furthers a society's moral ideal. Antipatterns: art prized only for formal beauty or aesthetic pleasure without moral effect; aesthetic theories conflating beauty with the good are rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must be universal and accessible to all
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should be accessible to everyone, not only an upper-class minority; if art is truly important it must be comprehensible and available to the whole people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy argues that the current exclusive art of the upper classes fails this test — it is costly, unintelligible, and socially limited. A test of true art: would the working masses be able to use and be elevated by it? Antipatterns: art that requires privileged education or leisure, or that exists only for an elite 'elect' (e.g., 'schöne Geister' or 'Übermenschen').

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility — art should be comprehensible to the general public
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal artist composes so that his work is intelligible to all men; obscurity and exclusive allusion are faults when they prevent understanding by ordinary people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy criticises modern trends that celebrate haziness, mystery, and deliberate obscurity (Symbolists, Decadents, Mallarmé, Verlaine, Baudelaire). Antipatterns: poems and prose that read like rebuses, reliance on mythological/historical allusions only initiates can decode, 'theory of obscurity' as a dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and naturalness — art must be neither affected nor artificial
rubrics_metrics.description: True art should be natural and sincere rather than affected, obscure, or 'brain-spun'; artificiality indicates decline of genuine art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy links exclusiveness and composing for a small, privileged circle to the rise of affectedness, euphemism, and deliberate cloudiness. Antipatterns: affected, contrived styles chosen to impress a limited audience, 'elevating' incorrectness and indefiniteness into merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness / novelty of feeling — art must transmit new feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine work of art brings new feelings into human life; art that only repeats known pleasures is not true art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy compares art to thought: real art, like real thought, transmits something not previously experienced. He cites how children are strongly impressed by works that first transmit feelings never before felt. Antipatterns: art focused on established enjoyment or hackneyed sentiment; formulaic repetition of pleasurable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter should be rooted in the broad life and religious perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The richest and most varied subject-matter for art springs from religious perception and the lived experiences of broad society (e.g., working people's life), not from the limited pleasures of idle classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy contends that religious perception yields endless fresh feelings (e.g., brotherhood of man), while the feelings of the idle wealthy are narrow (pride, sexual desire, weariness). He recommends drawing on the varied experiences of labor, struggle, community, and faith. Antipatterns: exclusive focus on aristocratic praise, erotic mania, melancholy, or trivialities of the idle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pleasure-as-default-criterion — enjoyment alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty or pleasure (the reception of enjoyment) cannot be the standard of what is good art; art judged only by pleasure is shallow and socially biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy traces the modern æsthetic theory that equates art with beauty/enjoyment to the loss of Christian moral ideals among upper classes and critiques it as arbitrary. Antipatterns: aesthetic theories that universalize an elite pleasure, or that claim ancient Greeks or Baumgarten vindicate pleasure as the essence of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusiveness and elitism in production and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing art exclusively for a small circle fosters obscure styles, incomprehensibility, and social corruption; true art should aim to communicate beyond an elite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy explains how composing for popes, courts, or a cultured crowd led artists to use allusions and euphemisms intelligible only to the initiated, escalating into a valued obscurity. Antipatterns: deliberate allusiveness, mystification, 'mystery' valued as proof of artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's subject-matter should elevate rather than pervert or degrade its audience
rubrics_metrics.description: If art, when understood by ordinary people, would pervert or fail to elevate them (e.g., eroticism that corrupts), it cannot claim to be true art for humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy argues that art of the wealthy classes often transmits feelings (honour, patriotism, amorousness as presented) that a working man would find bewildering or contemptible, or sexual content that would pervert rather than uplift. Use the test of effect on sincere, thoughtful people from broad classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of æsthetic dogma: do not conflate beauty, truth, and goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: The triad 'Beauty, Truth, Goodness' (das Schöne, das Wahre, das Gute) lacks definite meaning and obscures analysis of art; aesthetic theories that claim those terms are self-evident are misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy shows how Baumgarten's and later æstheticians' elevation of this trinity served to justify elite taste and disconnected art from moral/social purpose. Antipatterns: treating beauty as inherently morally good or using abstract capitalized concepts as a substitute for concrete evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should not intentionally sacrifice eloquence, clarity, or truth for 'mystery'
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposeful banishment of eloquence, passion, or exact truth in favour of vagueness or 'musical' effect is a fault when it obstructs sincere communication of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy quotes Gautier and Baudelaire and criticises the practice of degrading eloquence and truth to produce enigmatic works. Antipatterns: 'music before everything' taken to mean eliminating clear meaning; poems constructed to be puzzles (Mallarmé's 'always an enigma').
